rationale: This is essentially the net-share-issuance anomaly crossed with a standard Altman/Campbell-type distress score, and the product of two z-scores is maximal not only for distressed heavy issuers but equally for healthy non-issuers (both legs negative), a quadrant whose high expected returns directly contradict the stated negative sign.

The "costly voluntary deleveraging by distressed firms" mechanism is reasonably fresh, but the unsigned product means the same high signal value is produced by healthy firms raising net debt, whose returns should be low under the documented debt-issuance anomaly, so the expected positive sign is undermined by the mirror quadrant.

The costly-signaling mechanism (payout maintained under genuine near-term funding tightness rather than under leverage distress) is the most distinctive proposal here, though the author should note that negative working capital and low cash/current-liabilities also flag high-turnover, high-quality business models rather than stress, and that the low-payout/cash-rich quadrant loads with the same sign.

The 0/1 indicator makes this a genuinely state-contingent test with no sign-symmetry pathology, but it is close to the known composite external-financing anomaly conditioned on losses, and the large point mass at exactly zero will make decile portfolios lumpy and the spread hard to interpret.

A change-in-leverage × change-in-coverage interaction is plausible pre-distress dynamics, but the symmetric product assigns equally high values to deleveraging firms with improving cash flow — a clearly good state — so the expected negative sign fights the expression's own construction.

Largely redundant with proposal 1 and with the well-known issuance and profitability anomalies, and the discrete loss-count leg combined with the unsigned product means the top of the sort is dominated by profitable non-issuers (both z-scores negative), the group most likely to earn high returns.
